timeline.name: Vibro Champ
timeline.voice: A Champ with tremolo, and the tremolo isn’t where you’d expect.
timeline.story: Take a Champ and add Speed and Intensity knobs and you have a Vibro Champ: one 6V6, one eight-inch speaker and about six watts. Fender introduced it in 1964 and it went silver in 1968, which is the version here. The tremolo is the interesting part. On Fender’s AA764 drawing, the oscillator doesn’t touch the power tube’s bias. It works on the cathode of the preamp stage that drives the 6V6, and Fenderguru points out that no other black- or silver-panel Fender does it that way. Ours has the plain silver grille without the aluminum trim, which puts it from 1970 on. A black panel came back shortly before Fender stopped making it in 1982.
timeline.ratingNote: Catalog row 80, 6 W, 4 Ω class; the rear label on a 1978 amp reads 3.2 ohms. The catalog describes bias tremolo; Fender drawing AA764 shows the tremolo on the driver stage cathode (Q34). Cabinet 14.5 × 17 × 7.25 in from Mojotone; a dealer measures a 1969 amp at 14 × 17 × 7 in.

parts.label: Tremolo on the driver cathode
parts.title: The tremolo works on the preamp, not the power tube.
parts.body: Half a 12AX7 runs as a phase-shift oscillator, with Speed on a 3M pot. The Intensity pot, 25K, feeds that wobble into the cathode of the stage that drives the 6V6. The power tube itself isn’t modulated.
parts.listen: If the tremolo quits, look at the second 12AX7 and the driver stage, not the 6V6. That’s where the drawing puts it.
parts.together: Most Fender tremolos of the era either swing the output-tube bias or use a lamp and photocell. Fenderguru calls this arrangement unique among black- and silver-panel amps.
parts.detail: Our catalog row describes it as bias tremolo. The drawing doesn’t support that.
sources: Fenderguru: BF/SF Champ and Vibro Champ

parts.label: Single-ended 6V6
parts.title: One 6V6, no phase inverter.
parts.body: A single 6V6GT runs single-ended into the output transformer. It’s cathode-biased through a 470 Ω, 1 W resistor with a 25 µF bypass.
parts.listen: With one tube and no inverter, the amp gets to its breakup at bedroom volume. That’s why people record with these.
parts.together: Single-ended means the one tube handles the whole waveform, so there’s no push-pull cancellation of even harmonics.
parts.detail: Recording use is player lore, not documented by Fender.
sources: Fender: The legacy of the Champ

parts.label: Treble and Bass before the Volume
parts.title: The tone controls come before the Volume.
parts.body: The first half of a 12AX7 feeds a 250K Treble and 250K Bass stack, and the 1M Volume comes after it, ahead of the driver stage.
parts.listen: On a small amp you usually run the Volume high. The Treble and Bass shape what goes into the stage that gets pushed, so they change the breakup as well as the EQ.
parts.together: The stack uses a 250 pF treble cap, .1 µF and .047 µF caps and a fixed resistor for the middle.
parts.detail: The breakup point is our reading of the circuit.

parts.label: Negative feedback
parts.title: There’s a feedback loop from the speaker.
parts.body: A 2700 Ω resistor runs from the speaker output back to a 47 Ω resistor in the driver stage cathode.
parts.listen: Feedback tightens the bass and smooths the top a little. Owners who mod these sometimes lift it for a rawer sound.
parts.together: The tremolo signal goes into the same driver cathode.
parts.detail: The mod is common lore; not a Fender recommendation.

parts.label: Eight-inch speaker and back label
parts.title: An eight-inch speaker rated 3.2 ohms.
parts.body: One eight-inch speaker. Mojotone lists an Oxford 8EV at 4 ohms, and the printed label on a 1978 amp reads Speaker 3.2 Ohms, 6 Watts RMS. The back also carries a 1 A fuse and a jack for the vibrato pedal.
parts.listen: An eight in an open-back box is a big part of the small, focused sound.
parts.together: Fender’s drawing calls for a 1 A slow-blow fuse. The 3.2 ohm and 4 ohm figures describe the same class of load.
parts.extra: Mojotone field guide and a 1978 amp’s rear label.
parts.detail: Speaker brands varied through the run.
sources: Mojotone field guide: Silverface Vibro Champ

parts.label: Silver panel and grille
parts.title: The trim tells you the year.
parts.body: Mojotone says 1968 to 1969 amps have an aluminum trim strip around the blue-white-silver grille, and later ones don’t. The model shows the later look.
parts.listen: A trim strip is a quick way to spot an early silver-panel amp.
parts.together: Fender brought back a black panel shortly before the Vibro Champ ended in 1982.
parts.extra: Mojotone field guide; Fender’s Champ history.
sources: Mojotone field guide: Silverface Vibro Champ
Fender: The legacy of the Champ
